World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Down-to-earth Attenborough 'likes a glass of wine just like you and I'
World.content:
After a century on Earth, telling our planet's story, it's hard to find a generation not touched by Sir David Attenborough's life of work.

Whether it's his iconic voice, his infectious fascination with everything in the natural world or his passion to protect it, he offers something to most.

The legendary broadcaster and environmentalist turned 100 on Friday. Reflecting on Sir David's remarkable career, "timeless" is the word that comes to mind for personal friend and World Wildlife Fund UK CEO, Tanya Steele.

"I can't think of a generation alive today that hasn't heard or seen or has a feeling about David Attenborough," she told the ABC.

"But I think most of all, his voice. It penetrates, and we would recognise it anywhere in the world."

Tanya Steele has struck up a friendship with Sir David Attenborough. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

When Ms Steele met the British broadcaster 10 years ago, before he was about to give a speech, she remembered feeling a little daunted, given he's such a well-known figure.

"But I found him warm, well-informed and delightful company," she said.

What struck her about their first chance encounter was that he didn't want to talk about his speech. He wanted to discuss the plight of African elephants and her upcoming trip to Kenya.

"He was really concerned about drought conditions. So, he wanted to know what I thought the condition might be and the impact on wildlife," she said.

Sir David Attenborough turns 100: Celebrate his life in his words Natural history broadcaster Sir David Attenborough turns 100 today. We look back at his work and interviews to capture some of his wisdom and endless sense of wonder.

That moment stayed with Ms Steele and laid the foundation for what would become a close working relationship in her role as the first female CEO of the WWF.

"He's incredibly sharp. He's witty. I found David to be the same person wherever I have seen him," she said.

"The moments I've been privileged to spend time with him, he's absolutely someone that you enjoy spending time with."

Aside from being an "incredible storyteller", Ms Steele said Sir David was also great fun.

"He likes a joke; he likes a glass of wine like you and I. He is someone who is incredibly down-to-earth, and I think in many ways, he is really very humble," she said.

Sir David has worked alongside the WWF since it was founded in 1961.

Despite his deep involvement throughout his long and influential career, Sir David has always said he didn't start documenting wildlife to spark conversations; he simply enjoyed observing the natural world.

Sir David Attenborough visited Sydney's Taronga Zoo in 2003. (Reuters: David Gray)

Over the course of his lifetime, though, he's witnessed enormous changes to our natural environment, and as that's happened, he's shifted his message to those in power.

"Increasingly, David has spoken to audiences that carry more power and influence than most, and he's brought a very urgent message that we need to care for our natural world," Ms Steele said.

Using his stature and influence, he's sat down with world leaders, business CEOs, investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

"The changes we've seen in this world have been in his lifetime, one man's lifetime," Ms Steele said.

"He can chart the early days of places that we've never heard of, but that wildlife, those wild places, have disappeared, and he has brought a very personal message to people that actually, we can actually do something about it."

Over the course of his seven-decade career, Sir David has taken audiences to some of the most remote places on earth.

As a nod to his dedication to raising the importance of all things living, including those we've never heard of, he's had more than 50 animal and plant species named after him.

For his 100th birthday, London's famed Natural History Museum gave him another, adding a Chilean parasitic wasp to that long list.

Sir David's century on earth was ushered in with a week-long celebration by the BBC, where he began his career in 1952, while other fans offered their thanks in their own unique ways.

Artists in the English town of Morecambe marked Sir David Attenborough's birthday with a sand portrait. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

British composer Pete M. Wyer wrote a song for the occasion, inspired by Sir David's book A Life on Earth.

"I was in a slightly dark place. I was looking at what we're doing to the planet, which I found extremely disheartening," Wyer said.

"There were people saying, 'Oh, climate change is a scam, it's a hoax', and I was thinking, well, Sir David Attenborough doesn't say that, and I tend to trust his judgement. And so, it really began there."

After writing the song, he put out a call to everyone and anyone to send through their own rendition for a compilation, which was released on Sir David's birthday.

"I said, 'This is not about being a great singer. If you want to sing this, come and sing', and they did," Wyer said.

"The response has been amazing and chaotic and confusing and wonderful and utterly heart-melting."

An attendee records Sir David Attenborough's address at the 2019 World Economic Forum in Switzerland. (AP: Markus Schreiber)

From Africa to Europe to the US, he's received videos from fans across the globe and from all walks of life, including school children, octogenarians and people living with dementia.

"I think we should make him president of the world. He's the most unifying force on the planet," Wyer said

For those wanting to celebrate their love for one of the biggest icons of our time, sit back and relax, with most broadcasters rolling out his old takes for old times' sake.

But also to remind us of the momentous work he's done giving a voice to our natural world when humans haven't.

"There is no doubt that world agreements have been forged because of that message, because of that storytelling. Now, there's a great deal more to do, but unquestionably, I think David has played a pivotal role," Ms Steele said.

World.title: Regional housing crisis '25 years in the making'
World.content:
Owning your own patch of Australia, preferably with a quarter-acre block and a Hills hoist in the back, was the great Aussie dream.

Tired of city life, or priced out of the capitals, many Australians took their lead from country singer John Williamson and looked to the regions to find their home among the gum trees.

Now that dream is out of reach for many. So how did this happen, and could the upcoming budget fix the regional housing crisis?

The push to buy

Michael Fotheringham, managing director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, says this is a crisis 25 years in the making.

Michael Fotheringham says there are multiple factors that have lead to a housing crisis in the regions. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"There's a lot more pressure on regional housing markets right across the country," Dr Fotheringham said.

The Howard government's 1999 tax concessions for property investors turbocharged the desire for real estate, pushing people to buy property not just to live in, but to make money out of.

Prices climbed, a rise that was exacerbated in parts of regional Australia where there was a shortage of supply.

Tuesday's federal budget is expected to include a shake-up to tax breaks relied upon by investors.

For people such as disability pensioner Lara Howell, who is desperately looking for a house, change can't come soon enough.

Lara Howell is moving out because her rent will soon be too expensive. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"The amount of houses in the small country town that is Dunsborough [in Western Australia] that are clearly being owned as negatively geared investment properties that run on Airbnb or something equivalent is striking," she said.

" So for someone desperately looking for housing, you're driving past houses with five, six bedrooms, multiple bathrooms and they're completely empty and boarded up. "

Ms Howell said she understood why landlords were maximising their investment, but having so many vacant houses seemed absurd.

While country towns have historically had lower house prices, the housing crisis is felt acutely in the regions. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Why is it so expensive in the country?

Buying, selling and renting property in parts of regional Australia has now become more difficult than in metro areas.

Dr Fotheringham said there were several reasons for this, including property investors, migration of people from bigger centres to smaller towns and the impact of the COVID shutdown.

"Particularly during the COVID period, the lockdown period, we saw less people moving from regions to capital cities and more people doing the reverse," he said.

Housing shortages and high rents have been an issue in Dunsborough for many years. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

This push to the bush during COVID was deeply felt in communities like Dunsborough, where the price of rent has risen 80 per cent in the past five years.

Maiy Azize from not-for-profit Everybody's Home says regional areas are no longer immune from the housing crisis.

Maiy Azize says regional areas have been hit hard by the housing crisis. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

"You know regional areas were once upon a time a bit of a safe haven from cities. They are definitely not that anymore," she said.

"The capital gains tax discount has had a huge impact on affordability; it's brought a whole lot of investors into the market.

"We're hoping to see the federal government wind back these tax breaks for investors."

Lara Howell is packing up her unit right now because her rent has doubled in the past five years.

"I was paying $214.14 [in 2021], which was incredible," she said.

"I could have a life that affords meeting a friend for a coffee."

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to you ahead of the federal budget. Have your say.

The National Rental Affordability Scheme, a federal subsidy for owners of affordable housing, winds down at the end of June, which Ms Howell said would jack up the price of rent where she lived.

"All of these units in our little street will go back to full market value, which is up to anywhere between $585 and $600 a week, which, of course, anyone doing the maths on that will see that's not feasible," she said.

Social cost

Delilah Hatch, 23, lives in a granny flat at the back of her parents' house with her partner and their two-year-old daughter Layla in Bangalow in northern New South Wales.

Delilah and her daughter Layla know they can only buy their own home with the help of her parents. (ABC News: Hannah Ross)

The median house price in the Byron Shire, a property investment hotspot, has dropped back since its peak in 2022 and is now about $1.5 million.

The young mother says these sky-high property prices are limiting young people's life choices, including the decision whether or not to have children.

"I would ideally like to buy a house in this area, but I don't think it would be possible for me if I don't have help from my parents," she said.

"I will fortunately be able to inherit maybe housing from my parents one day. If I didn't have that, I think it would be impossible to buy back into this area.

"A few of my friends as well who have thought about having a family young have all said the same thing, that they would want to have a house first and they want to live in this area, which is why they can only imagine waiting a really long time before having kids."

Generational gap sparks appetite for change

Dr Fotheringham says we have reached a tipping point where the wealth gap between the generations is growing.

"We're seeing now settings that were put in place a generation ago that really helped that generation and are now continuing to help that generation at the cost of the next generation coming through," he said.

The Labor government proposed reducing tax concessions back in 2019, but Dr Fotheringham believes there is now a political appetite to make a change.

"They're showing the courage to do so now," he said.

The generation gap, explained Next week's budget will have the generation gap at its heart. But nailing down exactly what that gap is can be difficult. Here's what the evidence says.

"Increasingly what we're seeing is adults with younger children or even adult children and their kids can't get into the market the way they could.

"They are being less influenced by what helps them personally and are thinking more about what happens to the next generation.

"And that's the tipping point at which politically there's more to be gained by fixing the system than by maintaining those inequities."

Regional renters for life

Many young regional Australians have absolutely given up on the idea of home ownership.

Renting is what they're doing, but it's challenging because there simply is not enough stock.

Loading...

For Lucy, in Launceston in Tasmania, that has meant regularly moving from rental to rental.

"I'm 36 now, and I've only managed to really have one lease that was three, four years," she said.

"I've been moving around kind of every two, two and a half years for about, what's that, 17 years."

At 36, Lucy has moved from rental to rental for 17 years. (ABC News)

Alex Bomford, acting principal solicitor at the Tenants' Union of Tasmania, argues Commonwealth policy levers underpin the rental system across the country.

"Federal government policy means landlords are encouraged to make money from buying and selling houses, rather than through rental income from long-term tenants," he said.

"It shows that we see housing fundamentally as an investment tool, a speculation tool, rather than a place for someone to live."

Alex Bomford says short leases make life unstable for tenants. (ABC News)

Lucy is part of a generation grappling with lifelong renting.

"I remember being 27 and having a bit of a mental breakdown, realising that I probably won't ever own my own home," she said.

"There should be more understanding of what that experience is like."

Mr Bomford hopes changes in the budget might shake up our fundamental understanding of what a house is supposed to be.

"Housing in Australia needs to be built around actually housing people rather than as a vehicle for investment, as a vehicle to make money."

This sentiment is echoed by Dr Fotheringham.

He believes tax incentives have contributed to Australia's changing relationship with housing.

"Housing is about where we grow and shelter our families," he said.

"Property is where we grow and shelter our money and we've got to decide what those buildings are more about.

"Are they really more about the money or the people?

"And my view is that we should be putting people first in a way that's not destructive to the money."

World.title: Why Aung San Suu Kyi's son did not celebrate her move to house arrest
World.content:
When Aung San Suu Kyi's son heard his mother was being transferred from prison to house arrest, he didn't celebrate.

He hesitated.

"We have not had proof she is alive," said Kim Aris, who last received a handwritten letter from his mother two years ago.

"It was heavily censored, but she was able to convey her cell was extremely hot in summer and very cold in winter.

"She said her spirit remains strong, even if her health is not as good as it was in the past."

Aung San Suu Kyi's son has called for proof of life. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon )

The Nobel Peace Prize winner has been imprisoned since 2021, when Myanmar's military junta ousted the civilian government she led.

Last week, Myanmar's coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who was recently elected president in what has been widely dismissed as a "sham election", ordered the 80-year-old to be transferred from Myanmar's capital, Naypyidaw, to house arrest.

The military said the decision was "made to celebrate Buddha Day, to show humanitarian concern, and to demonstrate the state's benevolence and goodwill".

As part of the announcement broadcast by Myanmar state media, a photograph of Suu Kyi sitting on a bench, flanked by men in uniform, was shown.

A photo of Myanmar's detained former president Aung San Suu Kyi was broadcast on state media. (Myanmar State TV)

It is the first public image of her released in years.

But there were no details about where and when the image was taken.

Mr Aris, who lives in London, said he had seen no evidence indicating she had been moved.

He told the ABC that he had asked French President Emmanuel Macron and other governments to call for Myanmar to provide independently verified proof of life, and to provide her with access to medical care, her lawyers and her family.

"We have heard of my mother being moved to house arrest on a number of occasions over the past five years, and none of them have proven to be true," he said.

"The military have been playing these same games for over 30 years, and the world continues to fall for it."

Mr Aris said he had also been speaking to the British Foreign Office, but "no-one had been able to get any type of access to my mother".

'She will be over 100'

Suu Kyi was serving a 27-year sentence for a range of politically-motivated offences, ranging from incitement and corruption to election fraud and violating a state secrets law.

But, as part of a widespread pardon in April, her sentence was reduced by several years.

Mr Aris is worried the military's reduction of trumped-up charges against Suu Kyi is part of its efforts to seek legitimisation with the international community.

Mr Aris maintains that his mother was locked up under false charges.

"She should never have been in prison, so these aren't meaningful steps [to reduce her sentence]," he said.

Rumours of release and hope

About the time Mr Aris heard about Suu Kyi's move to house arrest, during the Myanmar Buddhist new year Thingyan, Chit Thein also started receiving congratulatory messages related to her father.

"Friends had heard rumours that my father was to be released," said Chit Thein, daughter of U Win Htein, a close aide to Suu Kyi and a member of her National League for Democracy party.

She allowed herself to hope.

During Thingyan, the Myanmar military tightly manages the release of political prisoners, while keeping others behind bars.

Family members wait outside prison for the release of prisoners in Yangon, Myanmar. (Reuters: Stringer)

But when the bus pulled out of Mandalay prison and was greeted by families eagerly waiting outside, Win Htein wasn't among those released.

However, what Chit Thein received a few days ago was a letter from her 84-year-old father.

Written in her father's hand were questions about his grandchildren and answering her frustration, and disappointment that he wasn't among those released.

"He said, 'I might not be able to see you and my grandkids anymore, don't expect too much,'" Chit Thein said.

Chit Htein is one of many family members of political prisoners waiting in agonising uncertainty. (Supplied: Chit Thein)

She said she noticed his tone reflected a Buddhist's calm acceptance of what may come.

"I want to write to him [to say], 'No, we don't give up,'" Chit Thein said.

"He can't stop me from hoping."

Among those released from the mass amnesty was Win Myint, who was serving as Myanmar's president until he was deposed in the military coup.

But more than 22,000 individuals, who were jailed since the military takeover, remain behind bars.

Aung San Suu Kyi pictured for first time in years Myanmar's detained former president Aung San Suu Kyi has been moved from prison to house arrest, according to state media.

The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar, a group of independent experts, said in a recent statement that "the junta is delivering half-measures aimed at placating ASEAN and the international community".

"A fake parliament headed by a fake 'President' in Min Aung Hlaing and more recently the junta's unverified claims to have moved State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi to house arrest, after years of solitary and incommunicado detention in conditions that likely constituted torture."

Myanmar's recent election was dismissed as a sham as dozens of parties were barred from running, including the National League for Democracy, whose government under Suu Kyi was overthrown in 2021.

Chit Thein said she welcomed calls from the Philippines and ASEAN Parliamentary for Human Rights for proof of life for Suu Kyi, but worries about the slow fade of international attention and fears the world will legitimise the brutal regime.

"People might forget because they don't see them in the media anymore," she said.

"Don't forget them, they are still inside prisons, it's a truth we can't forget."

World.title: Deaf and blind cricketers angered by changes to Cricket Australia's funding
World.content:
A decision by Cricket Australia (CA) to change how it funds inclusive teams has left many cricketers feeling disappointed, with some saying it could ultimately drive players away from the game.

Under the new arrangement, deaf and intellectually disabled men's cricketers, previously in separate national teams, will be combined into a single mixed disability team, with physically disabled players also brought into the fold.

A women's national mixed disability team will also be created.

An email sent to players late last year, seen by the ABC, acknowledged some "might be disappointed" but said they could still compete as separate teams overseas if they wished by "making their own arrangements and self-funding any tours or camps".

Members of Western Australia's blind cricket team at this year's National Cricket Inclusion Championships in Perth. (ABC News: Bridget McArthur)

At the same time, Australia's blind men's cricket team said its tour budget was in jeopardy.

Blind Cricket Australia (BCA) said CA had previously committed to funding one international series per year, but this arrangement had ceased, leaving the team's future roster up in the air.

CA told the ABC details of funding arrangements and tour schedules were yet to be confirmed but its financial commitment to blind and all abilities cricket remained strong.

It said it could not reveal how much money it put towards inclusion programs as it did not share details of commercial contracts.

CA is also conducting a review of domestic programs, including the National Cricket Inclusion Championship.

140 years of Deaf culture lost, says cricketer

Deaf cricket emerged in Australia around the early 1880s, making it one of the nation's oldest Deaf sports.

Played without hearing aids or cochlear implants, Deaf cricket created "a level and culturally meaningful playing field", which would be fundamentally altered in a mixed format, bowling all-rounder Callum Asbury said.

Callum Asbury says Cricket Australia's announcement has left many players feeling angry. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

He said the decision to merge the men's Deaf and intellectually disabled teams had "stirred feelings of anger, disappointment, confusion, curiosity, and in some cases, disinterest" among players on both sides.

"When players feel that their disability isn't being respected or represented, it can lead to people stepping away from the sport altogether — and that's a loss for everyone," he said.

Asbury said players learned of the change via email, with no prior discussion or warning, leaving them feeling dismissed and disrespected.

"Some players with intellectual disabilities may find it difficult, frustrating, or simply unengaging to learn Auslan, especially the specialised signs used in cricket," he said.

"That can unintentionally create a divide between the groups, making it harder to build cohesion on and off the field."

Callum Asbury says players weren't warned of the changes. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

CA said the majority of International Cricket Council nations supported moving towards a combined model, and the change was essential to remain aligned with India and England, where mixed disability teams have already been rolled out.

The England and Wales Cricket Board has confirmed it no longer funds the Deaf national men's team and has moved to a mixed model.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India has not responded to the ABC.

Both countries appear to still have separate Deaf cricket teams that are planning to attend the Deaf International Cricket Council's Deaf Cricket World Cup later this year.

Deaf Sports Australia, which strongly condemned CA's decision and said it had not been consulted, said Australia would not compete due to the national team no longer being funded.

CA argued the change would also make the sport a more viable candidate for inclusion in the 2032 Brisbane Paralympics.

However, International Paralympic Committee member Robyn Smith said applications were now closed for inclusion in the 2032 Games and, as far as she was aware, mixed disability cricket was not among the sports submitted.

Smith, who is also the president of the international governing body for elite intellectually disabled athletes Virtus, and Sport Inclusion Australia's international engagement adviser, said she was disappointed by CA's approach.

Victoria celebrates winning the Deaf and Hard of Hearing final at the 2024 National Cricket Inclusion Championships. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

"It's not a high performance pathway, it's tokenism from my perspective," she said.

The Deaf International Cricket Council, in a letter published earlier this year, similarly condemned the shift in some countries towards mixed formats.

"Deaf people are internationally recognised not solely through impairment, but by a shared visual language, culture, and lived experience," it said.

"This is why Deaf sport has never participated in the Paralympic Games."

Uncertainty around blind cricket tour roster

Changes to the blind program are unclear.

BCA chair Raymond Moxly initially told the ABC the national men's team would now only be funded to attend World Cups, which take place roughly every three years.

Raymond Moxly is disappointed by Cricket Australia's original proposal. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

He said it was understood the newly introduced women's blind cricket team would be on a similar triennial touring roster.

CA has consistently maintained that overall funding to inclusion programs had not fallen, but indicated some investment in the blind men's team may have recently been diverted to fund the blind women's team, which attended its first World Cup last year.

"Some of these programs fluctuate year on year depending on how we actually put our finite resources towards these programs to ensure equitability," CA head of community experience Jon Stimpson said.

Jon Stimpson says program changes aren't unusual. (ABC News: Nickoles Coleman)

Moxly, who used to play for Australia, said he was thrilled to see the women's program expand, but he did not think it should eat into the men's budget.

"Cricket Australia, I'm fairly certain, didn't change the amount of national touring that their men's team did when their national women's team was first introduced," he said.

"We'd love to see both teams given the opportunity to play annually."

Moxly estimated an international series costs around $200,000 to attend, "a drop in the ocean" for CA but a substantial fee for players, who would likely have to self-fund to maintain their previous touring roster.

He said the alternative was to settle for playing fewer games, which could see players lose motivation and potentially jump ship to other Para sports, which would be "hugely detrimental" to Australia's World Cup chances in 2027.

Since the ABC reached out to CA about the changes, Moxly said it had come back to the table.

He said a new proposal under discussion would see it fund a training camp and apparel next financial year for the men's and women's national teams, and one tour per year for each team for the following two financial years.

A formal agreement is yet to be signed.

Players feel confused, devalued

Star blind Australian batter Steffan Nero said many players had been anticipating potential cuts given CA's recent financial woes, and the ongoing uncertainty was frustrating.

Steffan Nero (right) is also unhappy with the decision. (Supplied: Steffan Nero)

This summer's Ashes series failed to relieve pressure, wrapping up quicker than expected, forcing CA to reimburse millions of dollars in unused tickets.

"I remember a few of the guys making jokes [during the Ashes] … saying, 'Well, there goes our funding for the next 10 years,'" Nero said.

" We always say … one step forward, two steps back. "

Nero said it was deflating given the team's recent performance in the inaugural blind Ashes series against England, which Australia won comprehensively.

How blind cricket's growth is making an impact across Australia Blind cricket provides an opportunity for blind or vision impaired people to participate in one of Australia's most popular sports, and find a sense of community.

He said it made the team feel more like a financial burden than an asset.

"We hadn't had that kind of series win and we expected things to kind of change and get better and stuff, and it's gone the complete other way," he said.

"This is not one-way. They benefit from it just as much as we have, probably more to be honest, with their marketing and social media."

CA promotes inclusion funding on its website, social media accounts and in advertising.

The tagline "a sport for all" has been a core pillar of its marketing strategy.

World.title: Mother's Day gratitude from a former foster child
World.content:
Unsure if he was lovable as a child, Jaharn recalls the dread he felt when Mother's Day was celebrated at school. Watching his friends greet and hug their parents while he remained alone was confusing.

One question dominated his thoughts: "Why don't my parents love me?"

That anxiety is no longer a concern for the confident 19-year-old, who grew up in out-of-home care and holds his own when advocating with some of Australia's most seasoned politicians.

There is certainty in the knowledge that his mum cares for him by choice and he lives in a home that is consistently secure and loving.

This Sunday, Jaharn Mundy-Drazevich will honour Selina Walker, the Ngunnawal woman who "became one of the strongest parental figures, not just in my life, but in the wider community".

"If she wasn't there, I honestly don't know where I would have ended up," said the Yuin, Ngunnawal and Ngarigo man.

"She didn't have to take us on, but she did."

Jaharn, as a young kid, soaking up the sun and surf on a family holiday. (Supplied)

At the tender age of two-months-old Jaharn was removed from his birth parents and then placed in a series of different foster homes. After an incident where he said he was badly burned, he found his way to his forever home.

Selina was 29 years-old when she made the decision to be a kinship foster parent.

"When I was told that they were going to have to go to foster care because I couldn't find any other kinship carers, that's when I decided that I would take [Jaharn] into my care," she says

Young Jaharn was accompanied by six closely aged relatives.

Settling in and building a family took more than a decade, according to the woman who raised Jaharn as a single parent.

Selina remembers that Jaharn's big lesson was "to let go of the parenting; that I was the adult".

"I had to demonstrate to him that I'm not going anywhere," she said.

"I'm not abandoning you. I look after the other [children] … so he could actually just be a kid."

Selina said being a foster carer was "not easy work".

"It is very tough trying to raise a traumatised child. But the reward is seeing them thrive and, like with Jaharn, wanting to give back [to the community]. This has been our cultural way for a very long time.

" It's just about supporting them to find their feet through the chaos. "

Now an adult, Jaharn (pictured here with Selina) wants to advocate for kids like him. (Supplied/ ABC graphics)

Selina has been a foster mother for more than 20 years and is currently the kinship carer of nine children.

The foster carer was recognised for her efforts in 2017 when she was named the ACT's Barnardos' Mother of the Year, and more recently when awarded the 2024 ACT Australian of the Year Local Hero.

Selina is a founding member of Yerrabi Yurwang Child and Family Aboriginal Corporation, a community-controlled organisation helping Indigenous families and children.

Winners are grinners! Jaharn said his childhood was better because of his foster mother. (Supplied)

Jaharn credits Selina as responsible for the young man he is today, through her unconditional love.

He is keen to work within the mental health sector with children and teenagers, having been inspired by Selina, he said.

"I'm on several youth advisory boards and groups now," Jaharn said.

"I want to do a bachelor's degree in social work and to work in the care and protection role or as a caseworker.

"I want to help them and be a stable guide and mentor."

Throughout his early life, there were times when dreams of university seemed beyond his imagination.

"I've gone through a lot of mental health challenges," he said.

" I always tell everyone that I'm a proud blackfella but growing up and not knowing who my family was and where we actually came from … that sense of identity wasn't always [as] clear as it is today. "

About seven years ago, he learnt of his Yuin heritage, from the south coast of NSW.

Jaharn hopes he can help children like his foster mother, Selina, has. (Supplied: SNAICC)

At a funeral for his grandfather two years ago, he finally met his aunties, uncles and cousins.

"That first real connection came through Sorry Business, which made the experience meaningful but also heavy."

Lived experience drives his advocacy to ensure all Aboriginal youth in out-of-home care and their carers are case managed by Aboriginal community-controlled agencies.

His passion to see young people maintain ties to their community saw Jaharn standing next to Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek at Parliament House, where they addressed a crowd in March this year.

Jaharn joined an alliance of organisations, including the national voice for Aboriginal children — SNAICC — to call on the government to urgently address the high rates of Indigenous children in out-of-home care.

Jaharn was invited to share at a Closing the Gap event. (Supplied: SNAICC)

Under the National Closing the Gap Agreement, all governments made a commitment to reduce the number of Indigenous youth in the system.

However, the latest data shows Indigenous children are about 10 times more likely to be in out-of-home care than other Australians.

Catherine Liddle the CEO of SNAICC also spoke at the event and said Indigenous families caring for Indigenous children is paramount.

"We know that children that are completely disconnected from their families are more likely to self-harm," she said.

"We know they're more likely to come into contact with juvenile justice systems. We know that it is a really hard road.

"There is a way to make that easier for children and that is by ensuring they have connections to who they are, and they know there are people behind them who love them for who they are."

Looking towards the future

Selina is proud of the young man Jaharn has become and is confident that he will be successful in whatever he wants to do in life.

"The proof is in the pudding and that's where you can see it in Jaharn ... [who has] become a strong, contributing Black man in society," Selina said.

Jaharn is also learning more about his culture and family connections, which he wasn't aware of while growing up in Canberra.

"Culture means a lot to me. Making those connections now, I've been able to do family history where I've been able to go back through generations … that's what I've always wanted," said Jaharn with a smile.

World.title: Some nannies working without superannuation due to 'discriminatory' law
World.content:
Despite working full-time hours as a nanny, Jess Renn has not been paid superannuation for more than two decades.

The Melbourne woman works up to 50 hours each week, typically across two families.

"I've worked [a maximum of] 30 hours [with] one family and 20 hours [with] another family, so that's where it has greatly affected me because [in] any other job, those are full-time hours," she said.

"But because I work across multiple clients, it then becomes an issue."

Under current laws, it is not compulsory for domestic workers employed in private homes, such as cleaners, housekeepers and nannies, working less than 30 hours a week, to receive super.

The 30-hour cap was originally introduced to prevent superannuation fund fees from eroding low-balance superannuation accounts.

But now, there are fee protections on small superannuation balances to ensure this does not happen.

Jess Renn has not been paid superannuation for more than two decades. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

When Ms Renn asked her employers about being paid superannuation, she said they told her they were not legally obliged.

"[With] one long-term family, I negotiated instead of a pay rise, I would salary sacrifice my pay rise into my super," she said.

"I realised I have maybe 25 per cent of super than any other person [at my age] may have in their bank right now."

Analysis from Super Members Council (SMC), the peak body for profit-to-members superannuation funds, shows nearly 40,000 domestic workers will be affected during the 2026–27 financial year, with each person missing out on about $4,000 a year, on average.

The lost superannuation adds up to nearly $150 million nationwide.

Super peak body calls for change to regulations

The council is calling for the federal government to scrap the "outdated and discriminatory" law. The change could leave domestic workers retiring with about $130,000 more in superannuation.

With women retiring with 25 per cent less superannuation than men, SMC said this change would help to reduce the gap, given 86 per cent of domestic workers were women.

Some domestic employees in private homes are missing out on superannuation. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"Domestic workers are doing essential paid work, yet the system still treats them as second-class workers when it comes to superannuation, and that burden falls overwhelmingly on women," said CEO Misha Schubert.

"When something is outdated, you fix it. Fixing these outdated laws would help close the gender superannuation gap and boost the retirement savings of thousands of hardworking Australians."

Workers try to catch up by making voluntary contributions

Another nanny, Ellen, who has asked the ABC to only use her first name, said one family she worked for made sure she never worked more than 30 hours a week.

The Super Members Council is calling for the federal government to scrap an "outdated and discriminatory" law. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"They would cut me bang on 29.5 [hours]. If it was looking like I was getting close, they'd go, 'Oh, go home', because they would not, they did not, want to pay me any super," she said.

Ellen said she tried to negotiate superannuation contributions with this family, but was knocked back.

"I confronted them, and they just bluntly said, 'Well, we don't legally have to because we keep your hours under 30 hours,'" she said.

" It took me years to negotiate my rate higher so that I could pay my own super. "

It has meant that she has missed out on years of employer contributions and compounding interest, which will ultimately affect her retirement.

"I am paying for that now myself by trying to bank an extra $50 a week into my superannuation so that I'm not falling behind … and I'm going to probably have to rely to some extent on my husband's superannuation and if I wasn't with him, I'd probably be in a lot of trouble."

The 30-hour cap on contributions was to prevent super fund fees eroding low-balance accounts. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

A 'power imbalance' between worker and family

Lauren Brown is the owner of payroll facilitation service Nanny Pay, which she said she created to ensure nannies were supported.

"This rule is leaving a loophole where people do not have to pay super, and … it just makes a wider pattern, and it makes it more complicated for people to do the right thing for their financial future," she said.

Lauren Brown says it is hard for nannies to financially prepare for their future. (Supplied: Lauren Brown)

Ms Brown said there was already a power imbalance between a family and a nanny, and the superannuation law exacerbated that.

"When the domestic super rule is the reason why families can say no, it makes that negotiation so much harder for that worker," she said.

"Women are already missing out on super because of maternity leave and raising children. It's just a systemic problem that this rule plays a big role in."

However, Mark Hudson, who is the managing director of another payroll facilitation service, Pay the Nanny, said he could see both sides.

Mark Hudson says nannies are being denied important employment rights. (Supplied: Mark Hudson)

"Lots of nannies might be doing two or three hours here and there, or might be a working-holiday maker," he said.

"Adding superannuation for someone like a working-holiday maker who's been here for a year, maybe only working 15 or 20 hours a week, adds the cost to the family, and it also adds complexity when they leave the country."

But ultimately, he said the law should be scrapped because it was contributing to a wider issue.

"It's pushing for giving them proper employment rights, so making sure people aren't having to get paid as a contractor or cash under the table and kind of more professionalising the whole industry," he said.

Both Ms Brown and Mr Hudson said the law was outdated, and many families using their platforms were already choosing to pay their nannies superannuation.

A spokesperson for federal Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said in a statement the government was aware of the issue and "remained committed to ensuring the superannuation system is providing Australians with dignity and security in retirement".

"The government continues to monitor the operation of workplace and superannuation laws to ensure they remain fit for purpose and operate as intended for all workers," the statement said.

World.title: Australians with motor neurone disease fear losing fast-tracked NDIS
World.content:
Australians with motor neurone disease (MND) who have rapidly changing needs fear they will lose a priority pathway to access the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) under the federal government's planned changes.

The federal government has been warned the support system helping people with MND must move "faster than their disease" or the caring responsibilities will fall back unfairly onto their families.

Currently people diagnosed with MND are able to access the NDIS via a priority pathway overseen by staff who specialise in the disease that approves support packages within seven days.

But advocates and patients have been unable to get assurances that this option will remain under a planned overhaul of the NDIS announced last month.

More than 160,000 people to be kicked off NDIS as Labor overhauls eligibility Health Minister Mark Butler has unveiled the government's plan to curb the ballooning growth of the NDIS and save the budget a projected $35 billion over four years.

By 2027 the government wants access to the NDIS to be determined by a person's functional capability rather than diagnosis.

The average life expectancy is about 27 months for a person diagnosed with MND, a rapidly degenerative illness with no cure.

MND Australia chief executive Clare Sullivan said the priority pathway to the NDIS had been a "game changer" and "must be protected".

"This includes an assessment from someone with expertise in MND, quick decisions for funding, and a package allocation that meets their overwhelming needs," she said.

" MND is an excellent case study for how the NDIS is working … but there is huge community concern about the mooted changes. "

Todd Johnson, 50, was diagnosed with MND four years ago and said the disease needed a "different model and rapid responses" from the system that is looking after people.

"People living with MND are losing function every week and the system has to move faster than the disease," he said.

"If it moves slower, families have to carry the cost and then the patients suffer and dignity's lost."

Nidhi fought for 10 years to get on the NDIS. New cuts leave her 'in limbo' Nidhi Shekaran is one of thousands of NDIS participants waiting to learn if their services will be impacted as part of sweeping government reforms to the scheme.

Mr Johnson said the under the current NDIS priority pathway he was able to quickly access additional support as his disease progressed.

"When I first got diagnosed I was still working and I was fully healthy and walking around," he said.

"Now I'm in a wheelchair and I need a bit of support for things like getting dressed … and even getting to the point where just rolling over becomes difficult.

"But because the NDIS has been responsive it's been a wonderful experience because I don't wait too long for things."

Mr Johnson, who is the president of MND Victoria, said people in the community with the disease were "very nervous and quite frightened" about potentially losing both the priority pathway and aspects of their package funding.

"When you consider the pathway might not be there, it's really concerning because a package that's right today might be dangerously inadequate in three months," he said.

"If we go back into the [mainstream NDIS] system it won't keep up with our needs and the speed of the progressiveness of the illness."

Health Minister Mark Butler said the government would be "engaging deeply" with the disability community on the reforms it intends to pursue later in the year.

Mark Butler says participants with high needs will have access to critical supports. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"The thresholds and assessment process for determining substantially reduced functional capacity will be developed in the second half of 2026 based on expert advice from a technical advisory group," he said.

"Participants with the greatest level of needs will continue to have access to critical supports needed to live well and with dignity."

The changes flagged by Mr Butler in April are designed to slow the NDIS growth from a projected $70 billion to about $55 billion by 2030.

In addition to stricter eligibility, Labor plans to impose caps on some participant spending and tougher rules for providers to combat fraud and rorting.

World.title: Coalition's EV strategy risks appearing out of touch
World.content:
Various echo chambers have been chuntering for some time about a generous federal tax discount for electric vehicle buyers.

It is, we've been told, an outrageous example of "middle class welfare".

Yet it's a policy the government this week confirmed will be largely kept on the books in Tuesday's budget.

It's a tax break that applies to novated leases, which allow car buyers to pay the interest, registration, insurance, maintenance and operating costs of a vehicle from pre-tax income.

The effect of which is to lower a worker's taxable income and thereby reduce how much income tax they pay.

On a traditional novated car lease, the benefit is subject to fringe benefits tax (FBT), which erodes much of the advantage of paying for the vehicle from pre-tax income.

When Labor won the 2022 election it soon delivered on a promise to exempt FBT as a way to incentivise EV uptake at a time when most consumers were still on the fence about their benefits.

This week the government announced it would gradually phase-out the benefit.

From April, it will be limited to EVs costing no more than $75,000, down from the current ceiling of $91,000. Two years later, FBT will be reapplied minus a 25 per cent discount.

When Labor won the 2022 election it soon delivered on a promise to exempt the fringe benefits tax as a way to incentivise EV uptake. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

EV sales go up

One of the stated policy goals at the time it was introduced was to accelerate the flow of EVs into the second-hand car market.

That's because novated leases tend to last for between two to five years. Once they end, many of the vehicles are onsold.

The underlying logic was that while the FBT exemption would be taken up mostly by people on higher incomes, when they rolled those cars into the second-hand market it would be to the benefit of lower-income households.

Which is what now appears to be happening, just as demand for EVs accelerates because of the war in the Persian Gulf.

Second-hand EV sales leapt by 138 per cent between February and March to 7557, according to data from the Australian Automotive Dealer Association.

The biggest selling second-hand vehicles in April were Tesla Model 3s and Model Ys, which were the most popular cars when the FBT exemption first set off a wave of new buyers in 2023 and 2024.

The data supports the notion that those same cars are now hitting the second-hand market, as intended, where they're selling for between $25,000 and $40,000. Other models are cheaper still, particularly when factoring in the lower operating costs of EVs.

EV tax discount removed two days' worth of carbon emissions Two days' worth of carbon emissions were removed thanks to the $2 billion electric vehicle tax discount. But its supporters say that put 64,000 more EVs on the road, jump-starting the struggling industry.

Despite driving more cars into the second-hand market, the FBT exemption still triggers outrage from some commentators and politicians.

According to the Nationals leader Matt Canavan the policy is a "completely failed scheme", a statement that overlooks the fact buyers have adopted it with far greater vigour than was anticipated a few years ago.

The government regards that as a success.

Canavan again: "Providing an electric vehicle subsidy through the tax system has meant that the only people who benefit are those that are on the top tax bracket.

"And it shows the priorities of the modern Labor party, that they're forgetting the workers.

"This is not just middle class welfare, this is upper class welfare."

Canavan's criticism no doubt tickles rusted-on EV haters, but its logic rests on a misconception.

For one thing, there's an erroneous notion that the FBT exemption "costs" the budget a huge sum of money.

Treasury estimates the revenue foregone from the FBT exemption will be about $1.4 billion in 2025-26, a figure that will rise to $2.8 billion in 2028-29.

But removing the FBT exemption does not mean the budget would suddenly be flush with those dollars.

That's because the exemption is one of the primary reasons people take out a novated lease to buy an EV.

If it didn't exist, many would either opt to buy an EV outright, without a lease, or they wouldn't buy one at all.

In other words, tax collected from a reintroduced FBT would likely be less than the exemption is currently "worth".

Any politician promising to "bank" all of the purported lost tax in their budget accounting is fudging the books.

Treasury recognises this reality by categorising its confidence in the estimate of dollars foregone as "medium to low".

Loading

Climate wars won via incentives

People who choose EVs do so for two primary reasons, according to a Redbridge poll (of 2,269 people who have a novated lease) that was taken in March and April on behalf of the National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association.

Number one, among the top three reasons nominated for buying an EV — at 65 per cent of those surveyed — was "saving money".

Next — at 57 per cent — was "qualifying for the FBT discount".

There's then a gap to the next reason, with 39 per cent "reducing dependence on petrol and diesel".

"Doing something for the environment" or "lowering carbon emissions" was 20 per cent and 29 per cent respectively.

Cost and the FBT exemption are the main catalysts, a finding that suggest the "climate wars" are being won quietly on incentives and technology rather than reactionary zealotry.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

If the benefits that underlie decarbonisation are better for consumers — cheaper, more reliable and less vulnerable to the consequences of military overreach by a distant ally — they'll embrace it.

Furthermore, interest in EVs appears to have become decoupled from political leanings, the Redbridge polling suggests, with significant implications for right-leaning parties.

It shows, unsurprisingly, some 96 per cent of Greens voters say they are "very/somewhat likely" to make their next vehicle an EV, followed by 92 per cent of Labor voters.

More notable is that Coalition voters are close behind, with 87 per cent mulling an EV.

And most surprising of all? Nearly three in four (72 per cent) of One Nation voters are eager to buy one.

The war in the gulf has demonstrated how reliance on fossil fuels can hurt lower income households the most.

Often in commuter suburbs where public transport options are poor, those same families are now seeking an alternative.

Many are conservative voters. Which risks making the Coalition's ongoing attempt to kill the FBT exemption look out of touch.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: Pentagon begins releasing decades of files on UFOs, unexplained phenomena
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Pentagon begins releasing decades of files on UFOs, unexplained phenomena Michael Koziol May 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Pentagon has started releasing what it says are “never-before-seen files” related to reports of unidentified flying objects (UFOs), including videos and photographs of phenomena captured from US military posts around the world. Many of the images published on Friday (US time) are murky black-and-white photos or video clips in which the purported flying object is unclear and resembles only a dot or black circle. Loading Others, however, show a more defined object. One brief clip taken from a US military infrared sensor in the East China Sea in 2024 purports to show a “football-shaped body” in motion. Another, taken from a censor in the Middle East in 2013, purportedly depicts “an area of contrast resembling an eight-pointed star with arms of alternating length”.



A note accompanying each clip declares that the description provided is for “informational purposes only” and readers should not interpret it as an analytical judgment, investigative conclusion, or factual determination. The Pentagon said the area of contrast “resembles a football-shaped body with three radial projections”. US Department of War Several images appeared to relate to the same purported sighting. The trove also contains declassified witness reports about object sightings going back to the 1940s. One recent report detailed an incident in which three separate teams of federal special agents purported to witness Orange “orbs” in the sky that emitted or launched smaller red “orbs” in groups of two to four, then disappear. These events were purportedly witnessed in the western US by multiple teams at various vantage points over the course of two days in 2023.



Another showed a site photo with a rendered graphic overlay which the Pentagon said depicted “corroborating eyewitness reports from September 2023 of an apparent ellipsoid bronze metallic object materialising out of a bright light in the sky”, which had disappeared “instantaneously”. The rendered graphic overlay of reports in September 2023. US Department of War The Pentagon – which last year imposed requirements on journalists that a court found were unconstitutional – said the files’ release was part of the Trump administration’s commitment to “unprecedented transparency” regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena - a modern term for UFOs. Defence Secretary Pete Hegeth said keeping the records classified had long fuelled “justified speculation” by the public, and it was time the American people saw the material for themselves. Additional files would be released on a rolling basis “as they are discovered and declassified”, the Pentagon said, with new tranches expected every few weeks.



US President Donald Trump urged people to draw their own conclusions about what they could see in the files. “In an effort for Complete and Maximum Transparency, it was my Honor to direct my Administration to identify and provide Government files related to Alien and Extraterrestrial Life, Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, and Unidentified Flying Objects,” Trump said on Truth Social. Related Article Exclusive

Space Want to visit space after Artemis II? For $20m, Anousheh flew herself there “Whereas previous Administrations have failed to be transparent on this subject, with these new Documents and Videos, the people can decide for themselves, ‘WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON?’ Have Fun and Enjoy!” Several files included military videos from the last several years that showed small ambiguous dots moving above the landscapes of Iraq, Syria and the United Arab Emirates. The white objects sometimes streaked across the screen in less than a second, while others slowly glided through the air or were followed by the camera.



Other documents included written reports from US military service members who were surveilling locations in the Middle East. One report described an object “shaped as a bouncy ball” and travelling 777 kilometres an hour consistently for at least seven minutes over Syria in 2023. The object was later determined to be benign. The Trump administration has previously released classified documents relating to the assassination of former president John F. Kennedy and civil rights activist Martin Luther King, but they revealed little information that was not already known. with AP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Get papped with your mum by one of Australia’s hottest photographers on Mother’s Day
World.content:
CultureArt & designPhotography Get papped with your mum by one of Australia’s hottest photographers on Mother’s Day Kerrie O'Brien May 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Atong Atem’s striking photographs reflect identity, family, history and politics. She often uses herself as a canvas, painting her face, and the images she creates are often a riot of colour, playful and almost always joyous. On Sunday afternoon, in a pop-up event designed for Mother’s Day, Melburnians will have a chance to get a portrait shot by Atem – with their mum. Photographer Atong Atem with her baby. Ruby Alexander That said, the 35-year-old mother of two says her definition of mother for the pop-up is deliberately loose. To her mind, there are plenty of places where people can celebrate their mum in “that traditional flowers-and-chocolates way”.



Atong Atem’s Maria of Mars (2022). Courtesy of the NGV “I want just one little space in the world where it’s not about that ... Not everybody has the same relationship to Mother’s Day or mothers and family in general,” she says. “My mental image is that it’ll be everything from a mum bringing in their newborn baby and taking a photo with them, to somebody who doesn’t even like their mum ... and wants to take a photo that their mum would hate.” She also welcomes people who’ve lost mothers or lost mother figures, encouraging them to bring in a photo and have “a beautiful portrait taken as they hold a photo, or that person’s favourite dress or hat, or something symbolic and personal”. People are invited to sit for a 10-minute portrait session and can take a signed print home for $50. The main response thus far, she says, has been from people who aren’t planning to have a literal photograph taken with their mother.



Initially, Atem assumed it would just be her immediate circle of people interested but already there’s been a huge response. Entertainment will be provided by her eight-year-old nephew, who is a musician. Visitors are encouraged to BYO garments or hats that might need freshening up, as there will be an embroidery service on site; a number of volunteers will be on hand to help. Atong Atem with her work at ‘PHOTO 2022’. Luis Enrique Ascui Raised on the Central Coast in New South Wales, Atem is now based in Melbourne. After escaping the second civil war in her parents’ homeland of South Sudan, the family spent time in Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya before arriving in Australia when she was six years old. Gallerist Andy Dinan of MARS Gallery recalls taking Atem’s work to Sydney Contemporary in 2019 and selling just one work; she cried on the plane on the way home. “Nine years on I’m laughing at how upset I was,” Dinan says.



Atem’s work has since been shown around the world, including at London’s Tate Modern, and is currently on display in Shanghai and Amsterdam. “[Atem’s work] is an examination of her displacement and also you can see her love of painting,” Dinan says. “She actually majored in painting and then went into photography, but you can see in her use of colour, how much she loves it. Atem’s “What we are given” (2024) was commissioned by the National Maritime Museum, Amsterdam. Atong Atem “She loves to photograph and is always working. She’s a delight to work with and her sense of community is second to none.” Dinan will take Atem’s new work to Sydney Contemporary in September and MARS will host a show in November.



In October, the National Gallery of Victoria will host a major survey show called Passage: The Art of Atong Atem. A world premiere, the exhibition will survey the past decade of her career, featuring more than 65 works. Related Article Literature How Shaun Tan’s book with no storyline inspired so many tattoos NGV director Tony Ellwood describes Atem as one of the most exciting artists of her generation, “redefining what it means to be Australian in contemporary life and culture”. “Her work aligns with the broader traditions of African studio photography, feminist aesthetics and diasporic storytelling. Yet, she has crafted a style and perspective that are uniquely her own, earning her recognition worldwide.” Atong Atem’s pop-up studio is at 99 Harding St, Coburg, from 1pm-5pm on Sunday, May 10.

World.title: Teals exploit donations gap in campaign to unseat Jess Wilson
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Teals exploit donations gap in campaign to unseat Jess Wilson Chip Le Grand May 9, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson will face a cashed-up independent challenger in her marginal seat of Kew for the first time after the funder of the teal movement, Climate 200, exploited a temporary gap in Victoria’s donation laws. Climate 200 co-convenor Simon Holmes à Court revealed to this masthead his organisation had tipped $40,000 into the campaign of independent candidate Sophie Torney, who is seeking to topple Wilson, and made a matching donation to Shima Ibuki, an independent running against former Liberal leader John Pesutto in Hawthorn. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson is facing a cashed-up challenger in her marginal seat of Kew. Luis Enrique Ascui The donations would have been illegal – and punishable by up to 10 years in jail – had they been made before April 15, when the High Court struck out Victoria’s campaign finance laws as unconstitutional. Under the previous regime, the maximum that any individual or organisation could donate to a candidate was $4970. There are currently no limits on the size of private donations to political candidates in Victoria, or any requirement for those donations to be disclosed.



The size of the Climate 200 contribution, which Holmes à Court said would be used to get the independent campaigns “off the ground” ahead of the November 28 election, will renew the urgency within the government and opposition to restore campaign finance rules. Related Article Updated

Victorian election Victorian election exposed after High Court strikes out campaign finance laws The Allan government had hoped to introduce legislation as early as Tuesday, when parliament next resumes, but is struggling to design a new framework that will satisfy its own caucus, win sufficient support within the parliament and withstand any further High Court challenge. Holmes à Court, who supported the successful High Court case of former independent candidates Paul Hopper and Melissa Lowe, defended Climate 200’s decision to make use of the regulatory vacuum. “Victorian taxpayers are funding almost the entire campaigns of their opponents, giving the majors a massive head start,” he said. “If we want remotely fair elections, we need to make sure challengers have adequate support to get off the ground.



“With just 202 days to the election, candidates can’t be expected to sit around and wonder how the state will clean up its mess.” He said he did not personally contribute to the donations. Centre for Public Integrity executive director Catherine Williams said Climate 200’s move underscored the need for the government to move quickly to restore transparency to the flow of campaign money. The Centre for Public Integrity is pushing for a restoration of disclosure requirements and public funding arrangements as an immediate step and the establishment of a more considered process after the election to develop a replacement campaign finance regime. “We anticipated that the period when Victoria lacked donations regulation was going to see an increase in the flow of money into campaigns,” Williams said. “That is the reason we want the government to at least restore transparency, urgently.



“What we ultimately want is for the parliament to put in place a comprehensive process to run post-election so this and other complex political finance regulation issues can be dealt with properly.” Premier Jacinta Allan has promised to backdate any changes to the Electoral Act to the day of the High Court decision. The influx of substantial donations into the teal campaigns in Kew and Hawthorn will reshape the contests in two of the Liberal Party’s vulnerable inner-city seats and invite further scrutiny of how Climate 200 funds community independents. Independent candidate Sophie Torney is running against Jess Wilson in the seat of Kew. Chris Hopkins Although Climate 200 is backed by high-worth individuals such as Holmes à Court, it says its electoral war chest is crowdfunding built from modest donations by more than 30,000 supporters.



It published an  in The Age on Saturday warning that this funding model, which it says involves average donations of just $33, would again be outlawed under the legislative fix being contemplated by the major parties. Holmes à Court has separately built an online portal titled “wall of advantage” which illustrates publicly funded benefits not available to independent challengers which incumbent MPs representing the major parties received to pay for political activities under the previous laws. He calculates that even in circumstances where a challenger is able to raise $250,000 in donations, they start more than $2 million behind a Labor or Coalition MP. Climate 200 founder Simon Holmes à Court. Oscar Colman David Feeney, a former Labor senator who recommended changes to Victoria’s campaign finance laws in a 2024 report, last week described the current vacuum as a regulatory catastrophe.



“The implications, unless a new system is established very, very swiftly, is that our November election becomes a billionaires’ picnic,” he told the Socially Democratic podcast. “What it means, in practical terms in November, is that teal independents, One Nation candidates – unless something changes – now have access to rivers of gold flowing into this state and into their political coffers.” Liberal MP David Davis went further. “It is hypocritical of the teals and Climate 200 to complain about donations when they are the first to make them,” he said. At the 2022 state election, independent candidates ran in Kew and Hawthorn but were kept campaign-poor by Victoria’s tight donation laws. Torney picked up 21 per cent of the vote in Kew, which Wilson holds by a margin of 4 per cent. Torney said the Climate 200 donation would get her 2026 campaign off the starting blocks.



“In Victoria, the major parties start every campaign with five to 10 times the resources of an independent and most of that gap is built from public money the major parties have funnelled to themselves,” she said. “That isn’t a fair contest.” The Victorian Trades Hall Council is also targeting the Liberal leader in her own seat, with a prominent billboard drawing attention to her party’s intention to preference One Nation candidates above Labor. Wilson says no decision has been made. Ibuki said the donation would make a material difference to her campaign in Hawthorn. “The High Court struck down the Victorian campaign finance laws for good reason, as the system rewarded the major parties and incumbents while putting huge barriers up against new independent candidate,” she said.



The High Court ruling centred on a carve-out under the old laws through which the major parties were able to receive unlimited campaign donations from legacy investment funds. The court found the arrangement, which was not available to smaller parties, new entrants or independents, was unfair and unconstitutional. The government, Liberal Party and Greens have agreed in backroom negotiations to reintroduce a cap on donations. There is no consensus on where the cap should be set, how much public funding there should be for political campaigns, and how to treat the legacy investment funds.
